claims.text: Binder jetting followed by a separate isothermal sintering step is an alternative to beam-based metal additive manufacturing.
AlCrFeNiSi powder can be successfully binder-jetted and consolidated by sintering at 1100–1200 °C.
The appropriate sintering atmosphere is argon or vacuum, with a hold time of 2–4 hours and slow cooling.
The proposed route is applicable to miniature AlCrFeNiSi coupons having 5–10 mm features.
Non-beam printing forms a binder-containing green body near ambient temperature rather than through melt-pool solidification.
Binder jetting eliminates rapid melt-pool solidification and the associated large thermal gradients during printing.
A subsequent isothermal sintering step can provide uniform densification and a structurally homogeneous alloy.
Avoiding the high thermal loads of laser melting reduces strain accumulation.
Diffusion-driven interdiffusion and isothermal sintering produce a homogeneous microstructure with low internal stress.
Binder-jet-sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have lower residual stress than laser-powder-bed-fused AlCrFeNiSi components.
Binder-jet-sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have higher ductility than laser-powder-bed-fused counterparts.
Binder-jet-sintered AlCrFeNiSi components will have yield strength comparable to or greater than laser-powder-bed-fused counterparts.
Non-beam extrusion and sintering can produce near-fully dense high-entropy-alloy structures with excellent mechanical properties.
AlCrFeNiSi powder in the approximately 15–50 μm size range is amenable to binder jetting.
AlCrFeNiSi parts larger than approximately 20 mm may require extended sintering or hot isostatic pressing.
Sintering AlCrFeNiSi above 1250 °C may cause grain growth or surface defects.
Slow cooling after sintering minimizes thermal gradients.
Residual stress can be compared by X-ray diffraction, while mechanical performance can be compared through tensile and fatigue testing.
Failure to obtain measurably lower residual stress or at least equal mechanical performance relative to laser-based parts would falsify the hypothesis.
